1.pericope_label: Hear my prayer, O Lord, and let my cry come unto thee... My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread

schools.summary: Delitzsch holds that the opening verses are unoriginal by design, being the familiar phrases of prayer that rise unbidden, and that only from the third verse does the psalm become its own; Ellicott says the same in a sentence and prefers brand or fuel to hearth.

Gill keeps the images personal, reading the days consumed in smoke as days spent in the obscurity of affliction; Calvin dates the psalm before the return rather than after it, restricts its use to those distressed at the Church's desolation, and finds in the title a play between the shutting up of grief and the pouring out of prayer.
Clarke assigns the psalm to the captives in Babylon and reads the wasting images allegorically, the Chaldeans being the fire and the captive Jews the fuel.

Henry reads it as composed by one afflicted with the church and for it, and calculated for others in like distress; Spurgeon makes the plea for a hearing the whole substance, since we might as well be atheists as believe in an unfeeling God.
Augustine asks who the poor man praying here is and answers that he was rich and for our sakes became poor, developing the riches at length before returning to the ashes eaten for bread.

debates.question: When and by whom was the psalm composed?

positions.view: By the captives in Babylon near the end of their oppression, the author unknown.
Before the return rather than after it, when deliverance was at hand and the prophets were beginning to comfort the people.
By one afflicted with the church and for it, and framed for the use of others in like distress.

debates.question: Are the opening phrases original to this psalm?

positions.view: No, and by design: they are the common phrases of prayer, and the psalm becomes original only from the third verse.
Prayer, like love, has its own language, which takes here the forms that meet us elsewhere.
The Holy Ghost has here drawn up the petition and put the words into our mouths.

outliers.note: Uses the title to argue that grief which shuts a man off from the sight of other men is the properest season for prayer, and rebukes his readers that scarcely one in a hundred is affected as he ought by the Church's calamities.
Alone identifies the poor man of the psalm with Christ, and reads the whole opening through the exchange by which he became poor that we might be rich.

themes: Hear my prayer, O Lord, and let my cry come unto thee.
Hide not thy face from me in the day when I am in trouble; incline thine ear unto me: in the day when I call answer me speedily.
For my days are consumed like smoke, and my bones are burned as an hearth.
My heart is smitten, and withered like grass; so that I forget to eat my bread.

5.pericope_label: By reason of the voice of my groaning my bones cleave to my skin... My days are like a shadow that declineth; and I am withered like grass

schools.summary: Delitzsch takes the ashes plainly, the mourner sitting in them and throwing them over himself, and reads the lifting up and casting down as God first removing the ground from under the man and then casting him from aloft, an emblem of Israel in exile; Ellicott defends the pelican against the objection that it is a water-bird, corrects the swearing to swearing by rather than against, and renders the closing figure a lengthening shadow.

Gill offers two etymologies for the pelican and settles on a bird of solitude, allows a second construction under which the psalmist ate bread like ashes, and distinguishes the apprehension of God's wrath from its reality, since Christ bore it in his people's stead.

Clarke identifies the birds loosely, takes the swearing as the Chaldeans binding themselves by oath, reads the lifting up as done so that the fall might be heavier, and finds in the declining shadow an allusion to the sun's southward turn; Wesley glosses the ashes and the cleaving skin in a line each.

debates.question: What are the birds of the wilderness?

positions.view: A pelican, defensible against the water-bird objection since the Hebrew word covers any open space and the bird does retire far inland; the second is an owl of the ruins.
A bird of solitude, whatever its species, which is why the psalmist compares himself to it.
Either the pelican or the bittern, and for the second some species of owl.
They swear by him, making his name a byword of execration.
They bind themselves by oath to destroy him, as men once swore not to eat until Paul was killed.
The reproach is continual, and good men should reckon it greater riches than the treasures of Egypt.

outliers.note: Answers the standing zoological objection to the pelican of the wilderness from the bird's actual habits, and elsewhere sets a modern poet beside the psalm's images.
Turns the verse about God's wrath inward, arguing that his people readily conclude they are under it but that this is their apprehension only, since Christ bore it in their stead.

themes: By reason of the voice of my groaning my bones cleave to my skin.
I am like a pelican of the wilderness: I am like an owl of the desert.
I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.
Mine enemies reproach me all the day; and they that are mad against me are sworn against me.
For I have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled my drink with weeping,
Because of thine indignation and thy wrath: for thou hast lifted me up, and cast me down.
My days are like a shadow that declineth; and I am withered like grass.

12.pericope_label: But thou, O Lord, shalt endure for ever; and thy remembrance unto all generations... When the people are gathered together, and the kingdoms, to serve the Lord

schools.summary: Delitzsch reads the turn as the promise's guarantee, the unchangeable God remaining when the church dies off on foreign soil, and places the argument's weight on the fact that God's own honour is bound up with the restoration, which becomes the means of the world's conversion; Ellicott makes God's eternity a pledge of the national hopes, and notices that this is the only place in the psalms where great events are said to be preserved in writing rather than orally.

Gill declines the exilic reference throughout, addressing the opening verse to Christ and referring the mercy on Zion, the stones and the destitute alike to the church of the latter day and under antichrist.

Clarke identifies the set time as Jeremiah's seventy years now ended, traces the historical steps by which the Gentile world was prepared for the gospel, and renders the destitute as one laid in utter ruin; Wesley glosses the remembrance from the divine name.

Henry balances the complaint with the permanence of God, insists that the set time is the best time because Infinite Wisdom appointed it, and takes the destitute for either a broken outward state or the broken spirit God looks for; Spurgeon notes that the Hebrew word is sit, so that God is enthroned to eternity.

debates.question: To what does the promised mercy on Zion refer?

positions.view: To the end of Jeremiah's seventy years, now come.
To the restoring of the church in the latter day, not to the Babylonish captivity.
To a time set by Infinite Wisdom, and therefore the best time, which Eternal Truth has fixed.
To a restoration whose fulfilment is urged upon God because his own honour depends on it.

debates.question: Who are the destitute whose prayer is regarded?

positions.view: Literally the naked one; the exiles stripped of home and rites, the word surviving in Arabic as the name of a stunted bush.
One laid in utter ruin and entirely wasted.
Either a low and broken outward state, or the low and broken spirit God looks for in all who draw near.
The church under antichrist, praying while the witnesses prophesy in sackcloth.

outliers.note: Observes that this is the only place in the psalms where the memory of great events is said to be preserved in writing, oral tradition being named everywhere else.
Traces the actual historical preparation of the Gentile world through the edict of Cyrus, the Greek translation of the Scriptures, and the dispersion under Rome.

themes: But thou, O Lord, shalt endure for ever; and thy remembrance unto all generations.
Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come.
For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof.
So the heathen shall fear the name of the Lord, and all the kings of the earth thy glory.
When the Lord shall build up Zion, he shall appear in his glory.
He will regard the prayer of the destitute, and not despise their prayer.
This shall be written for the generation to come: and the people which shall be created shall praise the Lord.
For he hath looked down from the height of his sanctuary; from heaven did the Lord behold the earth;
To hear the groaning of the prisoner; to loose those that are appointed to death;
To declare the name of the Lord in Zion, and his praise in Jerusalem;
When the people are gathered together, and the kingdoms, to serve the Lord.

23.pericope_label: He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days... The children of thy servants shall continue, and their seed shall be established before thee

schools.summary: Ellicott keeps the weakening to the course of an individual life, parallel to the shortening of days, grounds the prayer in the fear of not living to see the restoration, takes the perishing heavens as a wearing vesture, and corrects the closing verb from continue to dwell.

Gill insists that God and not the enemy is the weakener, reads the founding of the earth as proof of Christ's deity and against an eternal world, and holds that the heavens perish in quality and not in substance.

Clarke reads the weakening of the captives collectively, treats the prayer as the form they actually used, argues that whatever is not eternal must be perishable and finds the proof in the degeneration of seed, and says the Church is permanent because founded on God; Wesley reports the corporate reading and takes the prayer as one for Israel's survival until the Messiah.

Henry takes the weakened strength of the Jewish church as endangering the promise itself, defers to the apostle's application of the eternity verses to the Son, and infers the perpetuity of the body from the eternity of the head.

debates.question: Whose strength is weakened in the way?

positions.view: The psalmist's own, in the course of his life.
The Jewish church's, so that the promise of the Messiah itself seemed endangered.
The captives' collectively, brought so low that no restoration by their own efforts remained.
The whole commonwealth's, spoken of as of one man.

debates.question: In what sense do the heavens and the earth perish?

positions.view: Not as to substance but as to quality.
By being laid aside like an old garment, altered and not annihilated.
By necessity, since what is not eternal must be perishable, as universal deterioration shows.
As a vesture that wears out beside God's eternity, an image geology confirms.

outliers.note: Argues the perishability of creation from agriculture, since the same seed sown for several years running degenerates until it is not worth the labour of tillage, instancing wheat and the potato.
Follows the vesture image forward out of the psalm into a modern poet's lines on weaving the garment God is seen by, and thence into a later writer's philosophy of clothes.

themes: He weakened my strength in the way; he shortened my days.
I said, O my God, take me not away in the midst of my days: thy years are throughout all generations.
Of old hast thou laid the foundation of the earth: and the heavens are the work of thy hands.
They shall perish, but thou shalt endure: yea, all of them shall wax old like a garment; as a vesture shalt thou change them, and they shall be changed:
But thou art the same, and thy years shall have no end.
The children of thy servants shall continue, and their seed shall be established before thee.
